title: Why priority Queue is used in Djisktra's Algorithm
problemStatement: Dijkstra always expands the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance. Why must that selection use a priority queue (min-heap) — why isn’t a normal FIFO queue (BFS-style) enough?
example:
n = 3, src = 0
edges: 0→1 (1), 0→2 (100), 1→2 (1)

True distances: dist = [0, 1, 2]

FIFO queue that settles on first pop:
  queue after leaving 0: [1@1, 2@100]
  pop 1 → relax 2 to 2, push 2@2 → queue [2@100, 2@2]
  pop 2@100 and settle → dist[2]=100  ✗ WRONG

Min-heap always pops the smaller key first → pops 2@2 before the stale 2@100 → dist[2]=2 ✓
intuition: Dijkstra’s correctness needs “expand closest first.” A FIFO queue expands in discovery order, not distance order, so a farther tentative label can be settled before a better one arrives. A min-heap always gives you the current best unsettled label. (Bellman-Ford is a different algorithm for negatives — not a “brute Dijkstra.”)

approaches.title: Wrong: FIFO queue + settle on first pop
approaches.idea: Copy BFS: dequeue front, mark settled forever. With uneven weights the front is not the closest node → wrong distances.
algorithm: While queue: pop front (d,u); if already settled, skip; else settle u
Relax outs and push to the back
Bug: first time you see u may not be with the best d
approaches.code:
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def dijkstra_fifo_wrong(n, edges, src=0):
    """Demonstrates the bug — do NOT use in production."""
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in edges:
        g[u].append((v, w))
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    q = deque([(0, src)])
    settled = [False] * n
    while q:
        d, u = q.popleft()  # FIFO — not closest-first
        if settled[u]:
            continue
        settled[u] = True  # may freeze a BAD distance
        for v, w in g[u]:
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd
                q.append((nd, v))
    return dist

# dijkstra_fifo_wrong(3, [(0,1,1),(0,2,100),(1,2,1)], 0)
# → [0, 1, 100]  (should be [0, 1, 2])
approaches.dryRun: Settle 2 at 100 because 2@100 sits in front of 2@2 in the FIFO.
limitations: Works for unit weights (then it is BFS) — fails when weights vary

approaches.title: Slow but correct: scan for the min unsettled (no heap)
approaches.idea: Each step scan all unsettled nodes for the one with smallest dist — classic O(n²) Dijkstra. Same greedy idea, just a dumb “priority queue.”
approaches.whyWorks: Still expands closest-first; the scan is just a slow priority queue.
limitations: Fine for dense graphs / small n; heap wins on sparse graphs

approaches.title: Optimal: min-heap priority queue
approaches.idea: Heap stores (dist, node). Always pop the smallest tentative distance. Skip stale entries (d != dist[u]). That is the efficient closest-first selection.
algorithm: Pop (d,u); if d != dist[u] → stale, continue
Else settle / relax outs; push improved neighbors
Non-negative weights ⇒ first time d==dist[u] is final
approaches.time: O((n + m) log n) binary heap
approaches.dryRun: Heap order pops 1@1, then 2@2, then skips stale 2@100.
approaches.whyWorks: Min-heap = closest-first. Non-negative edges ⇒ no later path can improve a settled node.

python.notes: Priority queue = always expand the current closest unsettled node.

java.notes: PriorityQueue is the min-heap; ArrayDeque FIFO would break uneven weights.

specialTechnique.title: Interview answer (say this)
specialTechnique.body:
Dijkstra needs closest-first expansion.
• FIFO queue = discovery order ≠ distance order → can settle a bad label (wrong) or thrash.
• Array scan = correct closest-first but O(n²).
• Min-heap PQ = correct closest-first in O((n+m) log n).

Bellman-Ford is NOT “brute Dijkstra.” It is the right algorithm when edges can be negative (or you need negative-cycle detection). Dijkstra simply does not apply there.

complexity.time: O((n+m) log n) with binary heap

edgeCases: Unit weights → FIFO BFS is enough (special case of Dijkstra)
Stale heap entries (same node many times)
commonMistakes: Calling Bellman-Ford the “brute force” for Dijkstra
Using queue instead of priority queue on weighted graphs
Settling a node on first pop without d == dist[u]
patternRecognition: Follow-up after Dijkstra: “Why heap, not queue?”
followUps: Set-based Dijkstra (ordered set) vs binary heap?
When is O(n²) better than heap?
interviewInsight: One line: “The priority queue implements the greedy closest-first choice; a normal queue doesn’t.”
